# Hemostatic Clips and Clip Appliers

## Overview

Hemostatic clips and their associated clip appliers are medical devices designed to ligate bodily organs or tissues. A key feature of these clips is their ability to structurally conform to varying tissue thicknesses, ensuring effective and reliable closure across a range of clinical applications.

## Clip Structure

The hemostatic clip is constructed with two opposing arms—a first arm and a second arm—that are connected to one another at a shared joint portion. This joint is elastic in nature and maintains the clip in a normally-open configuration, allowing the arms to be positioned around the target tissue prior to clamping.

## Arm Configuration and Compression Mechanics

Each of the clip arms is composed of both outer and inner members. These members are equipped with tissue-contacting surfaces as well as intervening gaps. When the clip is applied, these gaps are able to elastically deform or shift, enabling the arms to accommodate different tissue thicknesses while consistently applying the necessary compression and clamping forces to achieve secure ligation.

## Locking and Interconnecting Features

To maintain closure once deployed, the clip incorporates a locking mechanism that secures the two arms together, preventing unintended reopening. In addition, the clip is designed with an interconnecting mechanism that allows multiple clips to be sequentially chained together lengthwise. This chaining capability facilitates efficient loading and successive deployment of clips during a procedure.

## Clip Appliers and Methods of Use

In addition to the hemostatic clips themselves, clip appliers designed for deploying the clips are also disclosed. Furthermore, methods for using these devices to ligate bodily organs or tissue are provided, describing the practical application of the clips in a surgical or clinical setting.

# Hemostatic Clips and Clip Appliers for Surgical Ligation

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates generally to surgical devices, and more particularly to hemostatic clips and associated clip appliers used for ligating bodily organs, vessels, ducts, or tissues during medical procedures. The disclosed devices are designed to provide secure, adaptable, and efficient ligation across a wide range of surgical applications.

## Background

During various surgical procedures, it is frequently necessary to occlude blood vessels, ducts, or other bodily structures to control bleeding or interrupt fluid flow. Hemostatic clips have long been employed for this purpose, offering surgeons a reliable means of ligation. However, conventional clips often present limitations in their ability to accommodate tissues of varying thickness while maintaining consistent, secure closure. A need therefore exists for improved clip designs that can conform to diverse tissue dimensions while ensuring dependable ligation.

## Summary of the Invention

The present disclosure provides hemostatic clips and clip appliers configured to ligate bodily organs or tissues with enhanced adaptability and security. The clips feature a pair of opposing clip arms connected at an elastic, normally-open joint. This joint incorporates both outer and inner members that are configured to elastically deform in response to closing forces. Through this cooperative deformation, the clip applies compression and clamping forces that conform to a broad range of tissue thicknesses, thereby ensuring an effective seal regardless of the dimensions of the target structure.

## Detailed Description

### Clip Arm Configuration

Each hemostatic clip comprises two opposing arms that extend from a common proximal joint toward their distal tips. In the natural, unstressed state, the arms are biased into an open configuration, permitting the clip to be positioned around the target tissue or vessel. Upon deployment, the arms are urged toward one another to grasp and compress the intervening tissue.

### Elastic Joint with Outer and Inner Members

A central feature of the invention is the elastic joint connecting the clip arms. Rather than relying on a single hinge element, the joint incorporates both an outer member and an inner member. As the clip arms are closed, these members undergo controlled elastic deformation. The outer member and inner member work in concert to store and distribute mechanical energy, allowing the clip to apply a continuous, resilient clamping force.

This dual-member arrangement enables the clip to accommodate tissues of differing thicknesses. When thicker tissue is captured, the elastic members deform to a greater degree, generating an appropriately increased clamping force. Conversely, thinner tissue receives a correspondingly modulated force. In each case, the elastic properties of the joint maintain sustained compression, reducing the risk of slippage or incomplete occlusion over time.

### Locking Mechanism

To ensure the clip remains securely closed after deployment, the design incorporates a locking mechanism. Once the clip arms have been brought together around the target structure, the locking mechanism engages to retain the arms in their closed, clamping position. This prevents inadvertent reopening and maintains consistent ligation throughout and after the surgical procedure. The locking feature works in cooperation with the elastic joint, complementing the resilient clamping force with a positive mechanical retention.

### Interconnecting Mechanism for Sequential Clip Chaining

The invention further contemplates an interconnecting mechanism that permits multiple clips to be sequentially chained together. This arrangement allows a series of clips to be loaded and stored in an ordered configuration, such that clips can be advanced and deployed one after another. The chaining mechanism facilitates rapid, repeated application of clips during procedures requiring multiple ligation points, improving surgical efficiency and reducing the need for manual reloading between applications.

### Clip Applier

Accompanying the clips is a clip applier configured to hold, advance, and deploy the interconnected clips. The applier engages the chained clips and delivers them individually to the surgical site, driving the clip arms closed and activating the locking mechanism upon deployment. The applier may be adapted for use in open surgical fields as well as in minimally invasive or laparoscopic procedures.

### Methods of Deployment

The disclosure also encompasses methods for deploying the hemostatic clips. In a representative method, a clip is positioned about the target bodily organ, vessel, or tissue with its arms in the normally-open configuration. The clip applier is then actuated to close the arms, causing the outer and inner members of the elastic joint to deform and apply a conforming clamping force. As the arms reach their closed position, the locking mechanism engages to secure the clip. Where multiple ligations are required, the next clip in the interconnected chain is advanced into position, and the process is repeated.

## Advantages

The disclosed hemostatic clips and appliers offer several notable advantages. The elastic joint with cooperating outer and inner members enables the clips to conform to a wide variety of tissue thicknesses while delivering consistent clamping force. The locking mechanism ensures secure, lasting closure, and the interconnecting mechanism supports efficient sequential deployment of multiple clips. Together, these features provide a versatile and reliable solution for the ligation of bodily organs and tissues across diverse surgical settings.
outputs.L5:
# The Hemostatic Clip

The hemostatic clip is a small but essential medical device used to control bleeding during surgical and endoscopic procedures. Designed to mechanically occlude blood vessels or close tissue defects, these clips have become indispensable tools in modern medicine, offering surgeons a reliable and efficient method of achieving hemostasis.

## What Is a Hemostatic Clip?

A hemostatic clip is a small metal or polymer device that compresses tissue or a blood vessel to stop the flow of blood. The clip works by applying constant mechanical pressure, effectively pinching off the vessel and allowing the body's natural clotting mechanisms to seal the area. Many clips are made from biocompatible materials such as titanium, which can safely remain in the body permanently, while others are absorbable and dissolve over time.

## Common Applications

Hemostatic clips are used across a wide range of clinical settings, including:

- **Surgical procedures:** Surgeons apply clips to ligate blood vessels during open and laparoscopic operations, reducing the need for sutures or cautery.
- **Gastrointestinal endoscopy:** During endoscopy or colonoscopy, physicians deploy clips to treat bleeding ulcers, close perforations, or mark tissue locations for future reference.
- **Emergency medicine:** Clips can rapidly control hemorrhage in critical situations where speed is essential.

## Advantages of Hemostatic Clips

The widespread adoption of hemostatic clips stems from several key benefits. They provide immediate and precise control of bleeding, minimize tissue damage compared to thermal methods, and reduce operative time. Their ease of deployment—often through a simple applicator device—makes them suitable for minimally invasive techniques. Additionally, titanium clips are generally compatible with imaging technologies, allowing patients to undergo MRI scans without complications in most cases.

## Conclusion

The hemostatic clip represents a simple yet remarkable innovation in surgical technology. By combining reliability, safety, and versatility, these devices continue to improve patient outcomes and support the advancement of minimally invasive procedures. As medical technology evolves, hemostatic clips remain a fundamental component of effective bleeding control across countless specialties.

# Patent Abstract

## Hemostatic Clip and Clip Applier for Ligating Bodily Organs and Tissues

A hemostatic clip and clip applier assembly is disclosed for occluding, ligating, and controlling bleeding in bodily organs, tissues, blood vessels, and other anatomical structures during surgical procedures. The hemostatic clip comprises a pair of opposing legs joined by a resilient hinge portion, wherein the legs define a tissue-receiving region therebetween. The inner surfaces of the legs include a plurality of interlocking features, such as complementary teeth, ridges, or grooves, configured to securely grip and retain the ligated tissue or vessel while resisting slippage and migration after deployment.

The clip applier includes an elongated shaft having a proximal handle assembly and a distal jaw mechanism configured to receive, hold, and deploy the hemostatic clip. Actuation of the handle causes the jaws to progressively close the clip legs about the target tissue, thereby applying uniform compressive force to achieve secure hemostasis. In certain embodiments, the applier is configured for single-clip or multiple-clip loading, enabling sequential deployment of a plurality of clips without removal of the instrument from the surgical site.

The clip may be formed from a biocompatible metallic material, a bioabsorbable polymer, or a combination thereof, permitting either permanent placement or gradual absorption following tissue healing. The assembly is adaptable for use in open, laparoscopic, endoscopic, and minimally invasive surgical applications. The disclosed device provides reliable ligation, reduces the risk of clip dislodgement, minimizes tissue trauma, and improves procedural efficiency during hemostatic and occlusive surgical operations.

# Technical Abstract: Adaptive Surgical Hemostatic Clip System for Variable Tissue Thickness

## Abstract

A surgical hemostatic clip system is disclosed comprising an adaptive ligation clip, a multi-fire applier, and associated methods for occluding vessels, ducts, and tissue bundles across a range of thicknesses. The system addresses limitations of fixed-geometry clips, which may provide inadequate closure force on thin structures or incomplete apposition on thick structures, thereby reducing the risk of clip slippage, tissue slicing, and post-operative hemorrhage.

## Clip Design

The clip comprises two opposing legs joined by a resilient hinge region fabricated from a biocompatible polymer (e.g., polyoxymethylene or polylactic acid derivatives) or a titanium alloy with elastic recovery characteristics. Each leg incorporates an inner engagement surface featuring a plurality of interlocking retention teeth arranged in a longitudinal series, enabling a ratcheting latch mechanism at the distal apex. This multi-position latch permits the clip to lock at progressive closure increments, accommodating luminal and tissue thicknesses ranging from approximately 0.5 mm to 5.0 mm within a single clip size. The inner faces present an atraumatic, radiused geometry that distributes compressive load uniformly, maintaining sustained occlusive pressure while minimizing focal tissue trauma and intimal disruption. An optional radiopaque marker facilitates postoperative imaging confirmation.

## Applier

The applier comprises an elongate shaft configured for both open and minimally invasive (laparoscopic/endoscopic) access, terminating in a distal jaw assembly that grips the clip legs during deployment. A proximal handle drives a progressive closure mechanism incorporating a tactile and audible feedback indicator that signals successful latch engagement at each ratchet position. In multi-fire embodiments, an internal magazine sequentially advances individual clips into the deployment jaw, enabling repeated ligation without instrument withdrawal. A force-limiting clutch prevents over-compression, while a lockout feature inhibits partial or misfeed deployment.

## Ligation Methods

The disclosed methods comprise: (1) positioning the open clip about the target structure; (2) progressively closing the applier jaws to advance the ratcheting latch; (3) monitoring feedback indicia to identify the closure increment corresponding to complete circumferential apposition without excessive compression; and (4) locking the clip at the tissue-appropriate position and releasing the applier. The adaptive latch thereby self-conforms to the encountered tissue thickness, ensuring consistent occlusive integrity across heterogeneous anatomical structures.

## Advantages

The system reduces intraoperative inventory by consolidating multiple fixed-size clips into a single adaptive design, decreases the incidence of clip dislodgement, and enhances procedural efficiency through multi-fire deployment and objective closure feedback.

---

*Note: This abstract is a technical drafting example. Specific material selections, dimensional ranges, and mechanism designs should be validated through engineering testing and regulatory review prior to any clinical or commercial application.*
